<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases and used the pressure round effectively, but the debate turned on one pivotal clash: whether CON's "remediation-on-notice, penalties for refusal" alternative is genuinely distinct from the motion's fine mechanism. PRO pressed this relentlessly from the opening rebuttal through closing, arguing that "repeatedly fails" already imports notice-and-correction logic (analogous to OSHA/tax abatement), so CON's model is simply a well-designed fine regime under a different name. CON's answer — that the distinction is "conduct vs. outcome," with the motion supposedly imposing strict liability even on good-faith actors hitting every milestone — depends on an unusually literalist reading of "repeatedly fail" that a neutral reader is likely to find strained, especially since CON's own alternative required the same milestones, deadlines, and correction windows that any sensible fine regime would include. PRO's closing crystallized this cleanly ("CON's alternative is PRO's case, minus the honesty to call it one"), and CON never fully escaped the charge. CON retained some unaddressed ground (small-provider remediation costs, the judgment-vs-binary enforcement gap for non-trivial accessibility criteria), which keeps the margin from being larger, but PRO's core structural argument was the more decisive and better-defended one across the exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange beginning with PRO's pressure question ("what is the operational difference between that penalty and the fine you're calling unworkable") and CON's answer distinguishing conduct-based vs. outcome-based triggers, resolved in PRO's closing charge that CON's model is "the motion, wearing a different label" — this was the decisive clash of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
